baseline_runs.answer:
Here's a simple way to explain it:

"Imagine you have a dollar, and at the candy store a candy bar costs one dollar. You can buy one candy bar. Now imagine that next year, the same candy bar costs two dollars. Your dollar didn't change, but now it can only buy half a candy bar. That's inflation. It's when things cost more money over time, so the money you have buys less than it used to."

If your cousin is curious, you can add: "Sometimes prices go up because lots of people want to buy the same things, or because it costs more to make them."

Here's a simple way to explain it:

Inflation is when stuff gets more expensive over time. Imagine a candy bar cost 25 cents when your grandma was little. Today, that same candy bar might cost a dollar. The candy didn't get any bigger or better. The money just became worth less, so it takes more of it to buy the same thing.

You can think of money like a bucket of water. Inflation is when the bucket gets a little leakier each year, so you need more water to fill it up.

Most of the time, prices go up just a little each year, and that's normal.

Here's a simple way to explain it:

"Imagine you have $5, and a candy bar costs $1. You can buy 5 candy bars. Now imagine next year the same candy bar costs $2. Your $5 still looks the same, but now it only buys 2 candy bars. That's basically inflation: prices going up over time, so your money buys less stuff than it used to."

If your cousin wants a fun follow-up, you can add: "Grown-ups try to keep prices going up just a little bit each year, because if prices fell instead, people would stop buying things and stores would have a hard time."

Here's a simple way to explain it:

---

Imagine you have **$5**, and at the candy store a chocolate bar costs **$1**. You can buy **5 chocolate bars**.

Now imagine that next year, everything gets a little more expensive. The same chocolate bar now costs **$2**. Your $5 only buys **2 chocolate bars** instead of 5. Your money didn't change, but it can buy less stuff. That's **inflation**.

**Inflation is when things slowly get more expensive over time, so your money buys a little less than it used to.**

Grown-ups try to keep inflation small, like a slow, gentle rise, instead of letting prices jump around wildly.

Here's a simple way to explain it:

---

Imagine you have a piggy bank with $5, and a candy bar costs $5. You can buy one candy bar.

Now imagine that next year, everything gets a little more expensive. The candy bar now costs $6. But your $5 is still just $5. So now you can't buy the candy bar anymore! Your money bought less than it used to.

That's **inflation**: when things slowly cost more money over time, so each dollar can buy a little less.

Why does it happen? Sometimes lots of people want to buy things at the same time, and stores raise prices. Sometimes it costs more to make things, so stores charge more too.

The good news is that grown-ups keep an eye on it so prices don't go up too fast. And a little bit of inflation is normal, kind of like how you grow a little bit every year!
